blocks.text: “Now is the day of salvation” is an urgent appeal to receive God’s grace rather than let it be fruitless. That urgency does not authorize crisis pressure, threats, sleep deprivation, or bypassing informed consent. Likewise, the hardships Paul lists commend endurance; they do not make suffering, poverty, hunger, sleeplessness, or beatings qualifications that leaders should reproduce.

Paul presents his speech and heart as open and asks the Corinthians to respond with comparable openness. The chapter’s movement from hardship and ethical commendation through its striking contrasts to this appeal can be read as a relational invitation. It does not turn a leader’s suffering into a claim on another person’s trust, contact, disclosure, affection, or reconciliation; the distinction between invited reciprocity and compelled vulnerability remains important.

Most of 2 Corinthians is preserved in P46, while P99 preserves portions; major codices provide additional witnesses with differing textual profiles. This is part of the wider textual setting for reading the letter.

The scope of the “unequally yoked” section remains disputed. It may concern idolatrous association, opponents, communal boundaries, or a separate letter unit; it does not directly name interracial marriage, interfaith marriage, business contracts, or friendship. Its temple and purity language cannot authorize treating people as contamination or enforcing racism, caste, misogyny, anti-LGBTQ coercion, or social isolation.
